[1] RCW 82.04.4461(5)(d): B&O TAX CREDIT FOR QUALIFIED
AEROSPACE DEVELOPMENT EXPENDITURES – A B&O tax credit is
allowed for “qualified aerospace product development expenditures.” The term
“qualified aerospace product development expenditures” includes only actual
expenditures documented in the ordinary course of business, and not estimates of
expenditures calculated under Internal Revenue Code Sections 41 and 174.
[2] RULE 254; RCW 82.32.070: BUSINESS AND OCCUPATION TAX
CREDIT - RECORDS – To claim a credit against B&O tax for qualified aerospace
product development expenditures, a taxpayer must provide documentation of
actual qualified expenditures. Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the
reader and are not in any way a part of the decision or in any way to be used in
construing or interpreting this Determination.
Headnotes are provided as a convenience for the reader and are not in any way a part of the decision
or in any way to be used in construing or interpreting this Determination.
NATURE OF THE CASE
Gabriella Herkert, T.R.O. – An aerospace manufacturing and research and development (R&D)
business protests denial of its request for refund based on a tax credit available for qualified
aerospace product development expenditures. We deny taxpayer’s petition.1
ISSUE
Under RCW 82.04.4461, RCW 82.32.070 and WAC 458-20-254 (Rule 254), did taxpayer
sufficiently document its research and development expenditures to qualify for an aerospace
product development expenditures tax credit against its business and occupation (B&O) tax?
1
Identifying details regarding the taxpayer and the assessment have been redacted pursuant to RCW 82.32.410.

Det. No. 23-0102, 45 WTD 054 (May 5, 2026) 55
FINDINGS OF FACT
. . . (Taxpayer) develops and manufactures aircraft structural materials Taxpayer engages in
research and development of aerospace products and materials. Taxpayer also engages in non-
aerospace manufacturing and development. In [City 1], Washington, Taxpayer designs,
manufactures and sells . . . components for the aerospace industry. In [City 2] Washington,
Taxpayer manufactures . . . components . . . for the aerospace industry. Taxpayer also engages in
non-aerospace activities.
On December 28, 2020, Taxpayer filed a request for refund. Taxpayer requested a refund equal to
1.5% of its expenditures from January 1, 2015, through October 31, 2020,2 that Taxpayer asserts
were qualified aerospace product development costs. Taxpayer supported its request with a federal
income tax survey it commissioned.3 Taxpayer admits it does not track expenditures to particular
business activities. Taxpayer did not provide documentation maintained in the ordinary course of
its business tracking expenditures to specific projects – manufacturing or R&D. Taxpayer
concedes it engages in R&D not related to aerospace, although Taxpayer contends it does so to a
much lesser extent.
The Department of Revenue’s (Department) Audit Division (Audit) reviewed Taxpayer’s books
and records for the tax period May 1, 2016, through October 31, 2020. On May 20, 2022, the
Department issued . . . Results of Your Recent Audit, showing a tax adjustment of $. . . .4 . . . The
Department denied Taxpayer’s refund request with respect to its claimed qualified aerospace
product development expenditures tax credit in the amount of $. . . . The Department’s denial of
Taxpayer’s refund request read in part:
You are not eligible for the requested aerospace product development credit due to
lack of substantiating documentation.
Taxpayer timely requested review. Taxpayer contends that the amount of gross income from
aerospace activities should be used as a proxy for the amount of expenses incurred in aerospace
product development. Taxpayer contends that the amount of gross income from its aerospace
activities can be verified using its excise tax returns.
2 . . .
3 The federal R&D study was commissioned by Taxpayer from its accounting firm . . . . A procedural manual provided
for 2013-2020 included an explanation of how qualifying labor and supplies were calculated in the studies. Such
expenditures were not actual, but calculated based on federal R&D methodology. Each procedural manual contained
a section called ‘Activity Documentation.’ For the 2017-2019 period, the section stated, “this documentation is
intended to demonstrate how the activities performed meet the legal requirements of IRC Sections 41 and 174.” No
reference is made to whether the activities qualify under Washington’s aerospace R&D credit, which is different from
the requirements of IRC Sections 41 and 174.
4 Taxpayer’s refund request was allowed for . . . sales shipped to Washington from out-of-state plants. Taxpayer’s
refund request was allowed for a personal property tax credit equal to personal property taxes paid on exempt
machinery and equipment (M&E) used in the manufacturing operation multiplied by a fraction for qualifying use.
Those portions of Taxpayer’s original refund request are not in dispute.

Det. No. 23-0102, 45 WTD 054 (May 5, 2026) 56
ANALYSIS
Washington imposes a B&O tax “for the act or privilege of engaging in business” in Washington.
RCW 82.04.220. The B&O tax measure and rate are determined by the type or nature of the
business activity in which a person is engaged. Chapter 82.04 RCW. The specific tax rate is
determined by the nature of the business activity in which a taxpayer is engaged. See generally
chapter 82.04 RCW.
The Legislature “intended to impose the business and occupation tax upon virtually all business
activities carried on within the state.” Simpson Inv. Co. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 141 Wn.2d 139, 149,
3 P.3d 741 (2000) (quoting Time Oil Co. v. State, 79 Wn.2d 143, 146, 483 P.2d 628 (1971)). The
B&O tax is not a tax on profit, net gain, capital gain, or sales “but a tax on the total money or
money’s worth received in the course of doing business.” Budget Rent-A-Car of Wash.-Oregon,
Inc. v. Dep’t of Revenue, 81 Wn.2d 171, 172, 500 P.2d 764 (1972). The B&O tax provisions “leave
practically no business and commerce free of the business and occupation tax.” Id. at 175.
. . .
RCW 82.04.4461 provides a B&O tax credit for qualified preproduction development expenditures
for aerospace product development activities, as follows:
(1)(a)(i) In computing the tax imposed under this chapter, a credit is allowed
for each person for qualified aerospace product development. For a person who
is a manufacturer or processor for hire of commercial airplanes or components
of such airplanes, credit may be earned for expenditures occurring after
December 1, 2003. For all other persons, credit may be earned only for
expenditures occurring after June 30, 2008.
(2) The credit is equal to the amount of qualified aerospace product
development expenditures of a person, multiplied by the rate of 1.5 percent.
(4) Any person claiming the credit must file a form prescribed by the
department that must include the amount of the credit claimed, an estimate of
the anticipated aerospace product development expenditures during the
calendar year for which the credit is claimed, an estimate of the taxable amount
during the calendar year for which the credit is claimed, and such additional
information as the department may prescribe.
RCW 82.04.4461(5)(b) defines “aerospace product development” as:
[R]esearch, design, and engineering activities performed in relation to the
development of an aerospace product or of a product line, model, or model
derivative of an aerospace product, including prototype development, testing,
and certification.

Det. No. 23-0102, 45 WTD 054 (May 5, 2026) 57
RCW 82.32.070 requires taxpayers to maintain records adequate for the Department to determine
their tax liability. RCW 82.32.070(1) states, in relevant part:
Every taxpayer liable for any tax collected by the department must keep and
preserve, for a period of five years, suitable records as may be necessary to
determine the amount of any tax for which the taxpayer may be liable. Such records
must include copies of all of the taxpayer's federal income tax and state tax returns
and reports. All of the taxpayer's books, records, and invoices must be open for
examination at any time by the department of revenue. . . .
Rule 254 is the Department’s administrative rule regarding recordkeeping. Rule 254(3) states, in
relevant part:
(b) It is the duty of each taxpayer to prepare and preserve all records in a systematic
manner conforming to accepted accounting methods and procedures. Such records
are to be kept, preserved, and presented upon request of the department or its
authorized representatives which will demonstrate:
(i) The amounts of gross receipts and sales from all sources,
however derived, including barter or exchange transactions, whether
or not such receipts or sales are taxable. These amounts must be
supported by original source documents or records including but not
limited to all purchase invoices, sales invoices, contracts, and such
other records as may be necessary to substantiate gross receipts and
sales.
. . .
(c) The records kept, preserved, and presented must include the normal records
maintained by an ordinary prudent business person. Such records may include
general ledgers, sales journals, cash receipts journals, bank statements, check
registers, and purchase journals, together with all bills, invoices, cash register tapes,
and other records or documents of original entry supporting the books of account
entries. The records must include all federal and state tax returns and reports and
all schedules, work papers, instructions, and other data used in the preparation of
the tax reports or returns.
Taxpayer contends it is entitled to the credit available for qualified aerospace preproduction
development expenditures under RCW 82.04.4461(2). The credit is equal to the amount of
qualified aerospace product development expenditures multiplied by a rate of 1.5 percent. Id.
Under RCW 82.32.070(1), Taxpayer bears the burden of maintaining documentation necessary for
the Department to verify its tax liability. Under Rule 254, Taxpayer’s documentation must include
source documentation including purchase invoices . . . .
In this case, Taxpayer did not maintain source documentation in the ordinary course of business
tying expenditures to actual business activities or segregating expenditures by project. Taxpayer
concedes that some of its projects are not qualified aerospace development so we cannot conclude
that any specific expenditure falls within the definition of “aerospace product development” in

Det. No. 23-0102, 45 WTD 054 (May 5, 2026) 58
RCW 82.04.4461(5)(b). Under RCW 82.32.070(1) and Rule 254, Taxpayer fails to meet its burden
to provide documentation allowing the Department to verify its purported tax liability, including
its claim for the aerospace development credit under RCW 82.04.4461(1)(a)(i). Moreover, using
a subsequent estimate of R&D expenditures, calculated under IRC Sections 41 and 174, not the
definition of “qualified aerospace product development expenditures” under RCW 82.04.
4461(5)(d), would impermissibly expand the application of the [credit]. Likewise, employing a
proxy method for estimating qualified aerospace product development expenditures, like the gross
income from aerospace development proposed by Taxpayer, instead of requiring a taxpayer to
meet its burden under RCW 82.32.070(1) and Rule 254, would impermissibly expand the pool of
taxpayers eligible for the credit. . . .
DECISION AND DISPOSITION
Taxpayer's petition is denied.
Dated this 9th day of May 2023.
